title: Decimal Reader
context: Grade 5, the page on reading and writing decimals. An adult sees two rules for saying a number. What the page is doing is tying each word to the digits it comes from, so that a decimal said aloud tells how big it is. Both readings are right, and a zero whole part may be read with zero and or without it.

writeup.why: Read a decimal in words both ways, with and and with point, and write a decimal from its words, with zeros in the empty places after the point.
writeup.look: Digit tiles over a place strip, two rows of reading chips under them, and a Words tray on the last phase.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Decimal Reader' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x sixty-four, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many chips the reading has so far, one for each word laid under the tiles. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x sixty-four, y 202. The digit tiles run across the working area at y 240, each 96 across with 12 between them, the large near-black point in its own narrow slot between the Ones and the Tenths. The place strip sits under the tiles at y 350, one name under each tile: Hundreds, Tens, Ones, the point, Tenths, Hundredths, Thousandths. The first reading's chips land in a row at y 430, the whole number part deep blue, the word and on the point, and the name of the last digit's place in amber under the last tile. The second reading's chips land in a row at y 520, the word point on the point and one word under each digit after it. Each row has a small speaker at its right end. The Zero and switch sits at x 110, y 620. On the last phase the Words tray runs along the bottom at y 640, its chips dragged up onto the place strip, and an empty place fills with a grey 0 labelled Place holder. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is a number pad of twelve keys with a point key, and a word pad of number words and place names, for setting a decimal or typing a reading into the answer slot. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the tools of this chapter share them. A decimal or fraction the question gives is deep blue, with the shaded parts that show it. The result the working reaches, a decimal, a fraction, a sum, a difference or what is left, is green, with its shaded parts. Ten of one place traded for one of the next, a carry in adding or a trade in taking away, is vermilion. A zero written after the point to line decimals up is violet, and so is the point written after a whole number before those zeros. The part taken away, used or poured out is rose. The digit, place or step being worked on now, and the first place where two decimals differ, are amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey, and nothing else on the stage is ever grey. An unshaded part stays warm white inside its near-black outline, the decimal point is near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label, Given, Answer, Carry, Trade, Added zero, Taken away, Left or Place holder, before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last decimal with both readings under it, the place of the last digit named in amber.

writeup.delight: On the first phase, as the last chip lands, the place strip's name under the last digit floats down and hooks itself onto the end of the reading in amber, and the voice reads the whole thing aloud.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with the tiles in place and no chips yet. On the first phase a decimal sits on the tiles over the place strip with the Read with and button lit. On the second the first reading is already built above an empty second row. On the third a decimal with a zero whole part sits on the tiles with the Zero and switch off. On the fourth the Words tray holds word chips and the place strip is empty. One thing moves, once: the lit button, or the first word chip, gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any decimal with up to three digits after the point, read both ways, with the Zero and switch and the Words tray. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on reading with and, reading with point, a zero whole part, and writing a decimal from its words.

source_tool.description: A row of large digit tiles sits across the upper half of the working area with a near-black point between the ones and the tenths, and a place strip under the tiles names each place: Hundreds, Tens, Ones, the point, Tenths, Hundredths, Thousandths. A Read with and button builds the first reading in chips under the tiles: the whole number part lit deep blue and read as usual, the word and dropped onto the point, the digits after the point lit together and read as one number, and the name of the last digit's place hung under the last tile in amber. A Read with point button builds the second reading in a row below: the whole number part, the word point on the point, and one word under each digit after it. Both readings stay up, each with a speaker so the voice reads it aloud. When the whole number part is 0, a Zero and switch shows the first reading with and without the words zero and, and both stay green. On the last phase a Words tray holds word chips; dragged onto the place strip they fill their places, and every empty place before the last one after the point fills with a grey 0 labelled Place holder. A number pad and a word pad set any decimal with up to three digits after the point. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many chips the reading has.
source_tool.art_direction: Digit tiles over a place strip / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: strips cut into ten equal parts, hundred grids of ten rows and ten columns, place value charts with a column for each place, column sums with their points in one line, and measuring jugs, ropes and scales marked in tenths.

Every whole is drawn the same size as every other whole it is compared or combined with, and its parts are exactly equal: a strip in tenths has ten parts of one width, and a hundred grid is always a full ten by ten.
The decimal point is drawn large and always sits between the ones and the tenths. In a column, every point lies on one vertical line.
A place value chart names every column above its digit: Hundreds, Tens, Ones, the point, Tenths, Hundredths, Thousandths.
Where shaded cells are counted, exactly the stated number is shaded, and they stay countable at a glance.

Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a strip cutting into tenths, ten tenths sliding together into one whole, a zero appearing after the point, or a carry moving to the next place.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit or a part the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a decimal plays in a piece of working: every decimal or fraction the question gives is deep blue, with the shaded parts that show it, and every result the working reaches, a decimal, a fraction, a sum or a difference, is green, with its shaded parts; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Ten of one place traded for one of the next place, a carry in adding or a trade in taking away, is vermilion. A zero written at the end, after the point, to make like decimals is violet, and so is the point written after a whole number before those zeros. The part taken away, used or poured out is rose. The digit, place or step being worked on now, and the first place where two decimals differ, are amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey. An unshaded part of a whole stays warm white inside its outline, and the decimal point itself is near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Carry, Trade, Added zero, Taken away, Left and Place holder, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Say the whole number part first. Then look at the point.
voice.onNext: A new decimal. Read it one way, then the other.
voice.opening: A decimal on the tiles, waiting to be read aloud.
voice.onFinish: Two readings of one number, and both of them right.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Read any decimal both ways, or build one from words.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: When the whole number part is zero

placement.where: After the class has read a few decimals from labels or headlines aloud. The tool is what ties each spoken word to its digits, and what fills the empty places with zeros when a decimal is built from words.

answer_key.rule: With and: read the whole number part as usual, say and for the point, then read the digits after the point as one number and name the place of the last digit. With point: read the whole number part, say point, then say each digit after the point on its own. Both ways are right. When the whole number part is 0, the words zero and may be left out. To write a decimal from words, the last word names how many places come after the point, and every empty place gets a 0.
answer_key.wrong: The reading is built again chip by chip under the digits, with the chip that differs from the child's lit amber, and the child's own reading kept beside it. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Read the whole number part as usual: three hundred twelve.
Read the digits after the point as one number: forty-six.
The last digit, 6, is in the hundredths place, so say hundredths.
items.answer: Three hundred twelve and forty-six hundredths
items.question: How is 312.46 read with and?
items.checkpoint: Read the digits after the point as one number, then name the place of the last digit.
items.misconception: Saying three hundred twelve and forty-six tenths, which names the place of the first digit after the point instead of the last.

steps: Read the whole number part as usual: nine.
Say each digit after the point on its own: three, zero, five.
items.question: How is 9.305 read with point?
items.checkpoint: With point, each digit after the point is said on its own.
items.misconception: Saying nine point three hundred five, which reads the digits after the point as one number in the point way.

steps: With and: the digits after the point are twenty-six, and the last one is in the hundredths place, so it is twenty-six hundredths.
The whole number part is 0, so the words zero and may be said or left out.
With point: zero point two six.
items.answer: Twenty-six hundredths, or zero and twenty-six hundredths; and zero point two six
items.question: Read 0.26 in both ways.
items.checkpoint: When the whole number part is 0, zero and may be left out. Both ways are right.
items.misconception: Reading 0.26 as twenty-six, which leaves out the name of the place and turns it into a whole number.

steps: Write 8 for the whole number part and put the point after it.
Thousandths need three places after the point.
Nineteen fills only two places, so write 0 in the tenths place first: 0, 1, 9.
items.answer: 8.019, which is 8 19/1000 as a mixed number
items.question: Write eight and nineteen thousandths as a decimal.
items.checkpoint: The last word names how many places come after the point, and an empty place gets a 0.
items.misconception: Writing 8.19, which is eight and nineteen hundredths, because the empty tenths place was not filled with 0.

items.final_answer: Four hundred fifteen thousandths, or zero and four hundred fifteen thousandths. Both ways are right

teaching_notes: Say every decimal both ways and accept either from the child: with and, the last digit's place names the decimal part; with point, each digit is said on its own. When the whole number part is 0, zero and may be left out; do not correct a child who says it or one who does not. Writing from words, the last word decides how many places come after the point, and every empty place gets a 0. The headlines are the child's own collection; read a few of their decimals aloud both ways in class.
generation_prompt: Build a decimal reading tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. Large digit tiles sit across the working area with a near-black point between the ones and the tenths, over a place strip naming Hundreds, Tens, Ones, the point, Tenths, Hundredths, Thousandths. A Read with and button builds the first reading in chips under the tiles, the whole number part in deep blue, and on the point, and the last digit's place named in amber under the last tile.
